title: Impact of Local Labor Demand Shocks on Wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Two-stage least squares (IV) using a Bartik (shift-share) instrument.
- Why: Local labor demand x is likely endogenous to wages y (reverse causality, omitted shocks). The Bartik instrument z—constructed from national industry growth rates interacted with pre-existing regional industry shares—provides plausibly exogenous variation in local demand that is unrelated to contemporaneous local wage shocks.
- Key assumptions:
  - Relevance: z is strongly correlated with x (first-stage strength).
  - Exclusion: z affects wages only through local labor demand x (not through other channels after controlling for observables).
  - Exogeneity: Pre-determined industry shares and national shocks are orthogonal to local idiosyncratic wage shocks.
  - Monotonicity: The instrument shifts x in the same direction for all regions (no defiers).
  - SUTVA: No cross-regional spillovers that violate stable potential outcomes.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Complete, self-contained R code for IV analysis with robustness checks

# 0) Setup ---------------------------------------------------------------------
req_pkgs <- c("AER", "sandwich", "lmtest", "car")
for (p in req_pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(p)
  }
}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(AER)
  library(sandwich)
  library(lmtest)
  library(car)
})

options(scipen = 999, digits = 4)

# 1) Read data -----------------------------------------------------------------
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s83_data.csv"
dat <- read.csv(path)

# Basic cleaning: ensure numeric, drop missing
num_cols <- c("y", "x", "z", "controls")
dat[num_cols] <- lapply(dat[num_cols], function(v) as.numeric(as.character(v)))
dat <- na.omit(dat)
n <- nrow(dat)

cat("Rows used:", n, "\n")
cat("Summary of key variables:\n")
print(summary(dat[num_cols]))

# 2) Helper to print robust estimates -----------------------------------------
print_robust <- function(model, vc, coef_name, label) {
  ct <- coeftest(model, vcov. = vc)
  if (!(coef_name %in% rownames(ct))) {
    stop(paste0("Coefficient ", coef_name, " not found in model."))
  }
  b <- ct[coef_name, "Estimate"]
  se <- ct[coef_name, "Std. Error"]
  tval <- ct[coef_name, "t value"]
  pval <- ct[coef_name, "Pr(>|t|)"]
  ci_l <- b - 1.96 * se
  ci_u <- b + 1.96 * se
  cat("\n", label, "\n", sep = "")
  cat("  Coef on", coef_name, "=", sprintf("%.4f", b),
      " (SE=", sprintf("%.4f", se), "), 95% CI [",
      sprintf("%.4f", ci_l), ", ", sprintf("%.4f", ci_u),
      "], p=", sprintf("%.4f", pval), "\n", sep = "")
  invisible(list(beta = b, se = se, ci = c(ci_l, ci_u), p = pval))
}

# 3) Baseline OLS (y on x + controls) -----------------------------------------
ols_formula <- y ~ x + controls
ols <- lm(ols_formula, data = dat)
ols_vc <- vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1")
cat("\n===========================\nBaseline OLS\n===========================\n")
res_ols <- print_robust(ols, ols_vc, "x", "OLS estimate")

# 4) IV (2SLS) with Bartik instrument -----------------------------------------
# Specification: y ~ x + controls | z + controls
iv1 <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = dat)
iv1_vc <- vcovHC(iv1, type = "HC1")

cat("\n===========================\nMain IV (2SLS) using Bartik instrument\n===========================\n")
res_iv1 <- print_robust(iv1, iv1_vc, "x", "Main IV estimate")

# 5) First-stage diagnostics ---------------------------------------------------
fs <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = dat)
fs_vc <- vcovHC(fs, type = "HC1")
cat("\nFirst Stage (x on z + controls):\n")
print(coeftest(fs, vcov. = fs_vc)["z", , drop = FALSE])

# Robust F-test for instrument relevance (H0: z = 0 in first stage)
lh <- linearHypothesis(fs, "z = 0", vcov = fs_vc, test = "F")
cat("\nRobust first-stage F-test for instrument relevance (H0: z = 0):\n")
print(lh)

# 6) Reduced form --------------------------------------------------------------
rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = dat)
rf_vc <- vcovHC(rf, type = "HC1")
cat("\nReduced Form (y on z + controls):\n")
print(coeftest(rf, vcov. = rf_vc)["z", , drop = FALSE])

# 7) Robustness checks ---------------------------------------------------------
# (a) IV without controls
iv0 <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = dat)
iv0_vc <- vcovHC(iv0, type = "HC1")

cat("\n===========================\nRobustness (a): IV without controls\n===========================\n")
res_iv0 <- print_robust(iv0, iv0_vc, "x", "IV (no controls)")

# (b) IV with nonlinearity in controls (add controls^2)
dat$controls2 <- dat$controls^2
iv2 <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls + controls2 | z + controls + controls2, data = dat)
iv2_vc <- vcovHC(iv2, type = "HC1")

cat("\n===========================\nRobustness (b): IV with nonlinear control (controls^2)\n===========================\n")
res_iv2 <- print_robust(iv2, iv2_vc, "x", "IV (controls + controls^2)")

# 8) Clear numerical result ----------------------------------------------------
cat("\n===========================\nKey Numerical Result\n===========================\n")
cat("Main IV estimate (beta on x):", sprintf("%.4f", res_iv1$beta),
    " (SE=", sprintf("%.4f", res_iv1$se), "), 95% CI [",
    sprintf("%.4f", res_iv1$ci[1]), ", ", sprintf("%.4f", res_iv1$ci[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("Robust first-stage F (relevance of z): ", sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(lh$"F")), "\n", sep = "")
cat("For comparison, OLS beta on x: ", sprintf("%.4f", res_ols$beta), "\n", sep = "")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
- Sign: Positive. Stronger local labor demand should raise wages.
- Magnitude: In typical Bartik wage applications, the IV elasticity/semi-elasticity often exceeds OLS due to attenuation bias from measurement error and/or negative selection. With variables scaled roughly in SD units (as preview suggests), expect an IV coefficient around 0.3 to 0.7. If x is a standardized demand index, a one-SD increase in demand increasing wages by about 0.4 to 0.6 SDs is plausible.
- Diagnostics: A robust first-stage F-stat comfortably above 10 would support instrument strength; reduced-form coefficient on z should be positive and significant if the mechanism operates through x. Robustness across specifications (with/without controls and with nonlinear controls) should yield similar positive estimates.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use Bartik shift-share as an instrument for local labor demand.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis reveals a significant positive effect of local labor demand on wages.
